full_text:
Once upon a time, a queen gave birth to a prince who was so misshapen and ugly that it was feared for a time he was scarcely human. He had a crooked spine, awkward limbs, and a comical tuft of bright red hair sprouting upon his crown. Yet as the queen wept over her newborn, a wise fairy who attended the birth comforted her, saying: 'Grieve not, Your Majesty. Your son shall possess so brilliant, charming, and profound a mind that no one shall notice his physical flaws. Moreover, I bestow upon him this supernatural gift: he shall have the power to impart the same measure of wit, eloquence, and intelligence to the person he loves most in all the world.'

Because of the comical red crest upon his head, the boy was named Riquet with the Tuft, or Ricky of the Tuft. As he grew, his words were so witty, his manners so courteous, and his wisdom so luminous that the greatest scholars and philosophers of the continent traveled to converse with him, enchanted by his companionship.

In a neighboring realm, another queen gave birth to twin daughters. The first was so astonishingly beautiful that the mother rejoiced, but the fairy present warned: 'She shall be radiant as the dawn, but she shall be equally dull-witted and lacking in sense.' The second twin was born remarkably plain, but the fairy granted her the gift of exquisite wit and charm.

As the years passed, the prophecies came to pass. Wherever the twin princesses went, people flocked at first to admire the dazzling beauty of the elder sister. But the moment she opened her mouth, her foolish remarks, awkward silences, and silly giggles drove everyone away to gather around the plainer younger sister, whose sparkling wit and delightful stories held the court spellbound. The beautiful elder princess wept bitter tears of humiliation, wishing with all her soul that she possessed half the intelligence of her plain sister, even at the cost of all her beauty.

One morning, having fled the palace to hide her shame, the beautiful princess was walking in a secluded forest when she encountered a short, misshapen gentleman dressed in magnificent courtly robes, wearing a distinctive tuft of red hair. It was Prince Ricky of the Tuft, who had fallen in love with portraits of her beauty and had traveled to her father's kingdom.

Seeing her weeping, Ricky bowed with courtly grace: 'Madam, how can a lady endowed with such heavenly beauty abandon herself to sorrow?'

'Alas, sir,' she replied heavily, 'I am as stupid as I am fair, and I would rather be the ugliest creature on earth if only I had wit and good sense.'

'Madam,' smiled Ricky, 'wit is not a gift that lies beyond your reach. I possess the fairy power to grant the highest intelligence to the lady I choose for my bride. If you will promise to marry me on this exact day one year hence, I will make you the wittiest and most charming woman in the world.'

Believing that a year was an eternity and that she might easily find a way out of the promise later, the foolish princess eagerly agreed. The moment she spoke her assent, a wonderful illumination flooded her mind. New thoughts, brilliant metaphors, and crystal logic blossomed in her understanding. She conversed with Ricky with such elegance, humor, and depth that she could hardly recognize herself.

Returning to the royal palace, the transformed princess stunned the entire court. Her father, the King, began consulting her on intricate treaties and statecraft; foreign ambassadors marveled at her diplomatic brilliance, and princes from every empire arrived to seek her hand in marriage.

A full year slipped away like a golden dream. Walking in the forest to ponder which of her noble suitors she should accept, she heard a strange rumbling beneath the earth. Kneeling by the grass, she saw the ground open to reveal an underground kitchen where hundreds of dwarf cooks were preparing an enormous wedding feast with spits of roasted partridges and cakes of sugar.

'For whom are you preparing this grand banquet?' the princess asked in surprise.

'For our master, Prince Ricky of the Tuft,' the head chef replied, 'whose wedding is to be celebrated tomorrow!'

The princess gasped; the year was up, and she had completely forgotten her promise! At that moment, Prince Ricky stepped from the trees, bowing low with love and devotion. 'I have come, fair princess, to claim the hand you promised me.'

The princess hesitated, troubled by her newfound intellect. 'Prince Ricky,' she said, 'when I made that promise, I was a foolish girl who understood nothing. Now that you have given me reason, how can you expect a wise princess to wed a prince who is so misshapen?'

Ricky smiled with gentle dignity: 'If I were a cruel, wicked, or foolish prince, you would have every right to refuse me. But is there anything in my soul, my character, or my devotion that displeases you?'

'No,' she confessed honestly, 'your character is the noblest I have ever met.'

'Then what stands between us except my outer appearance?' asked the prince. 'Did you know that the same fairy who gave me the power to make you clever also gave you the power to make the man you love handsome?'

'Is it true?' cried the princess. 'With all my heart, I wish that you may become the most handsome, noble, and well-proportioned prince in all the world!'

No sooner had she uttered the wish than the spell of love and magic worked its miracle. To the princess's eyes, Ricky's crooked spine straightened into a tall, athletic stature; his awkward gait became the majestic stride of a warrior; his comical tuft of red hair became waves of rich auburn locks, and his countenance shone with manly beauty and gentleness. (Some chroniclers whisper that the fairy magic did not change his limbs at all, but that the princess, having learned to love his noble soul, saw only beauty in the face of her beloved).

Together, they returned to the palace with joy. The King gladly gave his consent, and Ricky of the Tuft and his witty princess were wed in splendor, proving that love creates its own beauty, and that true affection sees through the eyes of the heart.
moral: True beauty is not merely skin deep; love and understanding transform the qualities of the soul into grace.
